events.title: Moxie Marlinspike releases TextSecure
events.summary: Whisper Systems launched TextSecure public beta on May 25, 2010 — Moxie Marlinspike's end-to-end encrypted SMS app for [Android].
events.about: TextSecure evolved into the Signal Protocol and Signal messenger — setting the standard for forward secrecy and encrypted messaging that WhatsApp and others later adopted. Marlinspike's open protocols influenced how developers think about E2E chat.

narrative.whyChosen: TextSecure started the modern era of consumer end-to-end encrypted messaging.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved usable E2E encryption could ship on mainstream mobile platforms.
narrative.problemSolved: SMS and early chat apps transmitted messages in plaintext readable by carriers and attackers.

events.title: Sass 3.0 adds SCSS syntax
events.summary: Natalie Weizenbaum released [Sass] 3.0 on May 10, 2010 — adding SCSS, a CSS-compatible superset syntax with braces and semicolons.
events.about: SCSS made every valid CSS3 file valid [Sass] — variables use `$` prefixes, mixins use `@mixin`/`@include`, but the surface syntax matches CSS. The change responded to Less's popularity and let teams adopt [Sass] without rewriting existing stylesheets or breaking editor tooling.

narrative.whyChosen: SCSS removed the biggest adoption barrier for [Sass]: an unfamiliar indented syntax.
narrative.whyImportant: It unified the preprocessor ecosystem around CSS-compatible supersets.
narrative.problemSolved: Teams with large CSS codebases could not justify migrating to [Sass]'s indentation-only format.

events.title: JetBrains PhpStorm 1.0 released
events.summary: JetBrains released PhpStorm 1.0 on May 27, 2010 — a dedicated PHP IDE with deep Symfony, Laravel, and Drupal support.
events.about: PhpStorm brought IntelliJ-grade refactoring, debugging, and Composer integration to PHP — the language behind WordPress, Drupal, and Laravel. It became the default paid IDE for professional PHP teams who outgrew generic editors but wanted more than syntax highlighting.

narrative.whyChosen: PhpStorm made JetBrains' IDE intelligence the standard for PHP web development.
narrative.whyImportant: It proved language-specific IDEs could win markets Eclipse and NetBeans served poorly.
narrative.problemSolved: PHP developers lacked an IDE that understood frameworks, templates, and mixed [HTML]/PHP files.

events.title: JetBrains WebStorm 1.0 released
events.summary: JetBrains released WebStorm 1.0 on May 27, 2010 alongside PhpStorm — a JavaScript and [HTML] IDE for front-end developers.
events.about: WebStorm targeted the jQuery and early SPA era with smart completion for JavaScript, CSS, and [HTML] — plus Node.js debugging before VS Code existed. It extended JetBrains' language-specific IDE line beyond RubyMine and PHP into everyday front-end work.

narrative.whyChosen: WebStorm brought IntelliJ-style editing to JavaScript before VS Code dominated the category.
narrative.whyImportant: It validated paid front-end IDEs in the age of TextMate and early Sublime Text.
narrative.problemSolved: Front-end developers used generic Java IDEs or text editors without JS-aware refactoring.

events.title: First real-world Bitcoin purchase
events.summary: Laszlo Hanyecz paid 10,000 BTC for two pizzas on May 22, 2010 — the first documented commercial Bitcoin transaction.
events.about: Hanyecz posted on Bitcointalk offering bitcoins for delivered pizza; Jeremy Sturdivant took the trade. The coins were worth pennies then and became a cautionary tale about early spending — but the event proved Bitcoin could settle real-world commerce, not just forum tips.

narrative.whyChosen: Bitcoin Pizza Day marks the moment cryptocurrency left pure speculation.
narrative.whyImportant: It demonstrated [peer-to-peer] digital cash could buy ordinary goods.
narrative.problemSolved: Bitcoin needed proof it worked as a medium of exchange, not just a curiosity.
